newsitem.title: UK: Dollar steadily softer in Europe, stg in spotlight.
newsitem.headline: Dollar steadily softer in Europe, stg in spotlight.

text.p: The dollar ended European trading softer on the day but stable, after a session spent in the rare role of sidekick to sterling.

The pound hogged the limelight, jumping to more than 4-1/2-year highs, after new UK finance minister Gordon Brown announced a rate rise and greater independence for the Bank of England. The tightening was expected; the central bank news was not.

"Dollar/mark was at first dragged up by the strength of the pound, which is unusual," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economist for Europe at BankAmerica in London. Comments from Bundesbanker Ernst Welteke later unsettled the U.S. unit, however.

Welteke, speaking on the fringes of a union meeting, said the Bundesbank was well advised to maintain its steady interest rate policy, and said the bank would not welcome a further rise in the dollar.
His remarks knocked dollar/mark down around a pfennig from near 1.73 marks. It was trading at 1.7219/27 marks at 1523 GMT, off a 1.7195 low, versus 1.7283/88 in late Europe on Monday.

News agency reports that Welteke had specified dollar/mark targets hit the dollar, although a spokesman later clarified the comments to Reuters. He said Welteke was happy with current levels though did not desire a significantly higher dollar.
Analysts remained upbeat on the dollar, however, pointing to April's 8,000 seasonally-adjusted rise in pan-German jobless, revealed this morning, as a negative for the mark.

"The data show the labour market is still not benefiting from what could be a nascent recovery in Germany. It'll take a lot more growth to put a dent into the unemployment trend," said Brian Hilliard, senior international economist at SGST.
Other German figures out today showed a 1.1 percent rise in March industry orders and an improvement in the April purchasing managers' index to 56.58 from March's 54.58.
Dollar/yen also fell during the European session, trading at 125.35/40 yen at 1552 GMT compared to late Monday's 126.41/46.
Increasing jitters about an interest rate rise in Japan helped the yen gain against both the dollar and mark in Asia overnight, while Japanese bond yields rose.
Mark/yen fell to 72.22/79 by 1558 GMT from Monday's late European level of 73.17/20.

The only data of note from the U.S. were March factory orders. They fell by 1.6 percent, slightly more than the consensus forecast of 1.4, and the February rise was revised down to 0.4 percent from 0.8. The dollar shrugged off the data.
For the rest, sterling outperformed after UK Chancellor Brown announced a quarter-point base rate rise to 6.25 percent before handing the monetary reins over to the Bank of England.
Under the Labour government's reforms, a new monetary policy committee will from next month set interest rates to meet an inflation target laid down by the government.
Previously, the Chancellor set interest rates after taking advice from the Bank of England.
Sterling hit 2.8330 marks -- its strongest since August 1992 -- in the aftermath of Brown's announcement, though had retreated to 2.8194/04 by 1607 GMT.
It finished European dealings around 2.8010/20 on Monday.
Against the dollar, the pound stood at $1.6365/75 in late Europe today, up from late yesterday's $1.6201/13 and not far below an intrasession peak of $1.6404.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
